tagline: River plains and rolling hills frame a highway with changing numbers.
intro: US 75 alternates between the Missouri River plain and rolling hills on Nebraska’s Lewis & Clark Scenic Byway. The Nebraska Department of Transportation lists 82 miles from just north of Omaha to South Sioux City. Visit Nebraska highlights cropland, wooded river bluffs and Native American culture along the scenic route. Near Dakota City, the drive uses a four-lane divided highway; south toward Homer, it narrows to two lanes as it follows the Missouri plain.

Lewis and Clark traveled up this Missouri corridor in 1804, and several former campsites lie near the highway. The US 75 number arrived on the Nebraska route north of Omaha much later. Previously, US 75 crossed into Iowa at Omaha; in 1984, the designation moved west of the river, replacing US 73 north of Dawson.

For a southbound drive, leave South Sioux City toward Homer, then climb from the river plain toward Winnebago and Macy. Macy is the tribal seat of the Omaha Reservation. At Decatur, descend to the edge of the plain and follow agricultural fields toward Tekamah, Herman and Blair. In Blair, US 75 shares Washington Street with US 30 for half a mile before their routes separate. Beyond Blair, continue to Fort Calhoun and the rolling hills north of Omaha.

moments.title: Winnebago
moments.text: The Winnebago Tribe’s buffalo herd has a pasture in the village, and its annual Homecoming Powwow takes place on the last full weekend in July. Winnebago lies within the tribe’s reservation in northeastern Nebraska. The village is called Nįšoc in the Hoocąk language; Ho-Chunk is the tribe’s name for itself. Both the village and its first post office, established in 1867, took their names from the tribe.

moments.title: Decatur
moments.text: A trading post at the mouth of Wood Creek helped shape Decatur, beside the upper Missouri River. Peter Sarpy helped lay out the settlement, which incorporated in 1856 as the Decatur Townsite & Ferry Company. Its name came from incorporator Stephen Decatur, a former schoolteacher who arrived in 1841. He called his farm Decatur Springs; its spring supplied the village with water for the next century. The Omaha had long occupied this country along the creeks and river before the town developed. After the townsite company dissolved, the settlement became Decatur Village in 1858.

moments.title: Fort Atkinson
moments.text: The fort at this state historical park is a reconstruction from the 1980s and 1990s. The original post’s beginnings were below the bluff: soldiers arriving in 1819 built Cantonment Missouri on the river bottom. After the Missouri flooded that camp in spring 1820, they built a permanent post atop Council Bluff and named it Fort Atkinson. Clark had recommended the bluff after the expedition’s 1804 council with members of the Oto and Missouria tribes. The Army abandoned the fort in 1827. The Nebraska Game and Parks Commission acquired the site in 1963, before undertaking the reconstruction; the park includes a military museum.
